name: Ratahan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sneddon, J.N. 1984. Proto-Sangiric and the Sangiric languages. Pacific Linguistics B-91. Canberra: ANU. (open online edition, DOI 10.15144/PL-B91)
catalog_quote: (2.1.5.2, p.24-25) Word stress is unpredictable and therefore phonemic. Stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable: kayu wood, ... house. In a large number o[f] words stress falls on the final syllable: sukol cough, tinik mosquito. Stress contrast is shown by the following pairs: mundupa to put and mundupa to measure a span, niu winnowing pan and niu coconut. One exception to the occurrence of stress on the penultimate syllable is when this syllable contains a high vowel and is immediately followed by another vowel in a closed syllable. In such cases stress usually falls on the final syllable. ... When stress occurs on a word-final high vowel the addition of a suffix may produce the conditions described above and, if so, stress shifts to the new final syllable, e.g. sumu nasal mucus + -an > sumuan having a runny nose. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is present verbatim (scanned spacing aside) in the Sneddon 1984 text we hold at sec. 2.1.5.2 pp.24-25, and the p.53 historical passage is also there; locator correct. (2) The classification 'lexical (default penult, many final; minimal pairs)' rests on a 1984 Pacific Linguistics comparative monograph by a fieldworker on the language; it is explicit, gives minimal pairs, and is the same source StressTyp2 uses, and the P;U database code is a coarsening of it rather than a contradiction. Nothing seen suggests the classification is wrong, and the historical account (stress shift off penultimate schwa followed by schwa replacement; CiVC shift followed by *h loss) independently explains why the contrast is lexical. (3) But the best available description is not yet obtained: Himmelmann & Wolff 1999 (Lincom LW/M 130, 126 pp) is the sole dedicated grammar sketch and is print-only
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: quotation verified in source, and now confirmed against page scan of the open PL edition. sources.note: The only dedicated description of Ratahan in Glottolog (126 pp, two fieldworkers, 15 years after Sneddon); its phonology section should state the stress/accent system synchronically (the title itself marks final stress on Toratán) and would either confirm 'lexical, default penult' or recast it (e.g. as contrastive vowel length/accent), and may describe stress under affixation beyond Sneddon's one -an example.

sources.note: Wolff uses Ratahan (own field data) as a witness language for PAn accent; the Ratahan section gives a synchronic statement of Ratahan stress/length contrasts and their regularity that would cross-check Sneddon's 'unpredictable' classification and the ST1 remark that long vowels, not stress, may carry the contrast.
